The US knew there was a threat to RAF Fairford - that's not in dispute here. The FPCON changes, armed patrol vehicles inside the base and concrete barricades all show that.

It seems possible to me that perhaps these 5 lads (or 8-10 if the eyewitness farmer is correct) were not actually there to attack the base - perhaps (given the fake fuel vans) they were actually in the area trying to steal fuel from local vehicles.

The farmer sees it, calls police. Police (who likely were aware of the USAF concerns) swarm into the area having perhaps not expected the "attackers" so soon. They manage to arrest 5 suspects and treat the 3 vans with every necessary precaution (as they should) - evacuating the neighbourhood, bringing Army EOD in, etc.

The males are initially arrested for Explosives Act offences (pending a safe way to check inside the vans) & go to custody. In the circumstances, further arrested for the Terrorism Act offence. However, after seizing whatever evidence they could (and examining the vans), it looks like police may have determined these aren't the attackers - as I say, potentially fuel thieves in the wrong place at the wrong time?

It's worth noting that if the terrorism act offences were looking likely, police could keep them detained for 48hrs initially before requiring a court to approve a longer period of time. Alternatively under normal arrest powers contained within the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984, they can be held for 24hrs initially (extended to 36hrs under authority of a Police Superintendent if specific requirements are met), and up to 72hrs if a further extension is authorised by a court. Now clearly if they were arrested in the early hours of Sunday morning and conveyed either to a local custody, or a dedicated counter-terrorism custody (likely closest in London), the fact they've been bailed today suggests they've spent at most 24-30hrs in custody before evidential review officers and the Crown Prosecution Service have determined there is insufficient evidence to charge them with an offence right now.

So they bail them with conditions not to contact each other as is normal procedure for vehicle interference/theft offences like that. But police need to download and analyse phones, and anything potentially seized from home addresses in order to ensure no link to the Iranian government or IRGC.

Meanwhile, did the actual planned attack get foiled inadvertently? Perhaps? Trump told the world that the US had been monitoring the "attackers" for some time - I'd suggest that if these lads genuinely were just in the wrong place at the wrong time, the actual suspects are now staying hidden until this all blows over a bit.

Either way, we don't have all the facts and that's part of any criminal or CT investigation - so yes, it sounds bad and arguably CTP could have done a better job of explaining it to the public, but they have to play their cards close to their chest right now in case my guesswork here is right and the suspects are still out there somewhere.

THE VIBE MANUFACTURING PLAYBOOK

1. Measure everything. Digital calipers for small parts, a phone LiDAR app like Polycam to scan a space or an object. Bad measurements are the #1 reason first builds fail

2. Have a frontier model write the design as code. Describe the part to a model like Claude Opus 5.5 or Astra, and have it write the design in a codebased CAD tool like OpenSCAD or CadQuery. Zoo's Text to CAD does it in one step!

3. Use real CAD files. The text to 3D models on Hugging Face make shapes that look right, but factories need precise files: STEP for machined parts, DXF for lasercut metal, STL for 3D printing

4. Make sure it can be made. Ask the AI to check the design against how factories actually work: how tight metal can bend, how small a hole can be, how much wiggle room parts need etc...

5. Prototype in plastic first. A $300 to $600 home 3D printer like a Bambu Lab lets you test the fit overnight before paying for metal (really fun to play with too!)

6. Pay an engineer for 1 hour. Before your first real order, have a mechanical engineer on Upwork etc review the files. It's the cheapest insurance you'll ever buy.

7. Send it out. SendCutSend cuts and bends metal, Xometry and Protolabs handle machining and plastic, JLCPCB builds circuit boards. Instant quotes, and parts usually ship in days.

8. Add the brains. Most smart features run on a cheap wifi chip like the ESP32. Design the board in KiCad, and use ESPHome to control it straight from your phone.

9. Make one, then fix it. Your first version will be off somewhere! Order a single unit, test it, and adjust.

10. Do the math. Add up parts, finishing, assembly, packaging, and shipping. Custom products are hard to resell, so price for healthy margins.

11. Sell the design and make to order. Let customers adjust the measurements, and only manufacture after they pay. Zero warehouse, zero unsold stock.

12. Handle the boring part. If it plugs into a wall or touches kids, you'll need safety certification. It's slow and annoying, which is exactly why it's a moat.

13. Scale when it works. Once orders are steady, switch to batch runs and your cost per unit drops fast.

Control the Badge, Not the Model: A Conservative Framework for AI Agent Security

Saturday, October 3, 2026
Dr. Joel Rutkowski
Policy Paper

Developed from Julio Rivera, “What Is the Real AI Cybersecurity Threat?” (October 1, 2026, https://t.co/4m5RSjfVj7), from Executive Order 14409, Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security (June 2, 2026), and from the operational record on agent identity, prompt injection, and critical-infrastructure risk through 2026.

Executive summary

Artificial intelligence is becoming an actor, not only an advisor. Systems that can read mail, call tools, change permissions, and move money create a cybersecurity problem older than the technology: authority granted beyond the task. A Cloud Security Alliance survey released in April 2026 found that 53 percent of responding organizations had seen AI agents exceed intended permissions and 47 percent had suffered an agent-related security incident in the prior year. Only 16 percent were highly confident they could detect an agent-specific threat. Only 8 percent said agents never exceeded scope.

The binding failure is not model intelligence. It is over-permissioned identity, indirect prompt injection, and standing credentials. The conservative response is least privilege for non-human actors, short-lived credentials, human approval for consequential actions, voluntary public-private vulnerability coordination, and criminal enforcement. Executive Order 14409 already points in that direction. It establishes an AI cybersecurity clearinghouse and a voluntary framework for covered frontier models, and it states that nothing in the order authorizes mandatory licensing or preclearance. This paper converts that principle into an operational agenda. It does not create a permit to build a model.

The problem

Capability and authority are different objects. An assistant that summarizes a document poses a different risk from an agent that can read customer records, alter account permissions, send email, modify databases, and execute commands. The underlying model may be similar. The blast radius is not.

Three conditions make the difference operational.

First, agents act. Adoption has moved ahead of governance. Industry surveys in 2026 find production agents authenticated with static Application Programming Interface-API keys, shared service accounts, and inherited user sessions, and only a minority of organizations maintain a real-time agent inventory. A default cloud service identity can carry the same defect. The March 2026 disclosure of over-scoped permissions on a Vertex AI project service agent showed that ordinary metadata-service credential theft, not a novel exploit, was enough to reach data and move laterally inside a project.

Second, untrusted content can carry instructions. Prompt injection, ranked by Open Worldwide Application Security Project -OWASP as the leading large-language-model application risk since 2023, exploits the absence of privilege separation inside the model’s context. An email, web page, ticket, or retrieved document can induce an agent to use tools it was given. Case reviews of publicly documented agent incidents find excessive privilege and indirect injection together in a large majority of events, and a bypass or absence of human approval in essentially all of them. Input filtering reduces noise. It does not bound damage.

Third, speed multiplies scope. A compromised employee is limited by working hours and attention. An agent with the same permissions moves across systems continuously. Hospitals, banks, utilities, and other critical operators inherit the pattern if an efficiency tool is given standing control of the system it is meant only to observe. Criminal misuse is already measured. The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center warned in December 2024 that generative systems make impersonation and financial fraud easier to scale. The 2025 Internet Crime Report, released in 2026, recorded 22,364 AI-related complaints and nearly $893 million in reported losses.

The policy error would be to treat these facts as a reason to license model development. Offenders do not apply for permission. Defensive models are delayed by the same preclearance that is supposed to restrain offensive ones.

Guiding principles

Authority is not capability. Intelligence does not justify access. An agent is a contractor with a badge, not a new employee with the master key.

Least privilege and fail-safe defaults apply to non-human actors. Saltzer and Schroeder’s 1975 principles—least privilege, complete mediation, fail-safe defaults, separation of privilege—remain the correct design rules. NIST SP 800-53 (AC-6) and zero-trust guidance (NIST SP 800-207) already state them.

Zero trust is a control, not a slogan. No implicit trust from network location or from the label “AI.” Authenticate and authorize per action. Assume the agent can be manipulated.

Innovation and defense are complements. Voluntary coordination and criminal enforcement protect infrastructure without making government permission a prerequisite for release. Mandatory licensing would trade unmeasured safety for slower defense.

Liability follows the grant of authority and the criminal act. Deployers who give reckless standing scope, and persons who use tools to commit unauthorized access or fraud, are the responsible parties. The existence of a model is not.

Measurement honesty. Survey prevalence is not verified national loss. Both should be reported. Detection confidence and inventory coverage belong in the same account as incident counts.

Policy recommendations

Give every production agent a distinct identity and a named human owner. Prohibit shared service accounts and borrowed user sessions for tool use. Credentials should be short-lived, attestable where the platform allows, and revocable in one action.

Scope rights to the task and default to deny. A scheduling agent does not receive payroll, customer databases, or payment authority. Agents that read untrusted content do not receive outbound write tools. Sandbox retrieval from mail, the web, and documents.

Require human approval for consequential actions. Thresholds set by the deployer should cover payments, production changes, permission changes, and release of sensitive data. Log every tool call and retain an audit trail sufficient to reconstruct an incident.

Inventory agents in near real time. An agent that cannot be listed cannot be revoked. Assign monitoring responsibility explicitly, including at smaller firms that begin with restricted permissions, confirmation steps, and tested backups.

Bound critical infrastructure. AI may detect fraud, flag vulnerabilities, and support operations only through controlled interfaces, with independent monitoring and tested recovery. It does not receive standing authority over safety or control systems.

Implement Executive Order 14409 without enlarging it into a license. Stand up the AI cybersecurity clearinghouse with industry and critical-infrastructure operators. Use the voluntary pre-release framework for covered frontier models, with confidentiality, insider-risk, and intellectual-property terms. State in statute that no mandatory licensing, preclearance, or permitting requirement is created for development or release. Direct the Attorney General to prioritize unauthorized access, wire fraud, and impersonation committed with AI tools. Fund vulnerability-discovery research through existing grant mechanisms.

What this framework does not do. It does not require government approval to train or publish a model. It does not claim that prompt injection has a reliable content-filter solution. It does not create a national AI commission. Sector regulators and contracts can require the identity controls above.

Evidence in brief

Access control is not a 2020s invention. Bell-LaPadula (1973) formalized clearance and classification. Saltzer and Schroeder (1975) stated least privilege and fail-safe defaults. The Orange Book (1985) made identification and audit conditions of trust for government systems. Federal Information Security Management Act-FISMA (2002) and National Institute of Standards and Technology Special Publication-NIST SP 800-53 carried those rules into federal risk management. The Target breach (2013) and the OPM breach (2015) showed credential theft plus excessive internal trust. NIST SP 800-207 (2020) and Executive Order 14028 (2021) made zero trust, software transparency, and incident reporting explicit.

Agentic systems change the actor. Systematic reviews through early 2026 find the attack surface shifting from direct jailbreaks to indirect injection, tool hijacking, and retrieval poisoning, while defenses still cluster at input filtering. The April 2026 Cloud Security Alliance survey supplies the operational warning: scope violations in 53 percent of respondents, agent-related incidents in 47 percent, high detection confidence in 16 percent. Default cloud identities have produced the same class of failure without a novel exploit. FBI reporting establishes criminal use as a present fraud channel, not a hypothetical.

Implementation

Sequence the private-sector controls first, because they reduce blast radius whether or not a clearinghouse is fully staffed: unique identity, task scope, short-lived credentials, human gates, logs, inventory. Federal systems should apply the same standard through binding operational directives already contemplated by the June 2026 order. The clearinghouse coordinates scanning, validation, and prioritized remediation. It does not approve models. Frontier evaluation stays voluntary and classified. Prosecution uses existing computer-fraud and wire-fraud statutes. Procurement and sector guidance can require agent identity standards for vendors serving hospitals, banks, and utilities without a new statute licensing developers.

Risks of implementation. Global criminal tooling will keep improving synthetic impersonation even if domestic agents are tightly scoped. A clearinghouse that becomes a de facto approval desk would contradict the order’s text. Firms that inventory agents but leave standing privilege will meet the letter and miss the control. Survey figures will be attacked as vendor-commissioned. The correct reply is to pair them with incident logs and to avoid claiming a national loss total the data do not support.

Conclusion and Final Thoughts

The AI cybersecurity debate will be decided by who holds authority, not by how capable the model becomes. Rivera’s question—what happens when an agent can do something it should never have been allowed to do—is the correct framing. Intelligence is not the failure mode. Permission is. An assistant that summarizes documents and an agent that can change account rights, send mail, move money, and execute commands may share a model. They do not share a risk. The April 2026 Cloud Security Alliance findings make the gap operational rather than theoretical. Those figures are survey prevalence, not a national loss census, and they were commissioned in a vendor market. They are still a warning. Adoption is outrunning identity governance. Default cloud service accounts, shared API keys, and inherited user sessions turn a manipulated instruction into lateral movement. The Vertex AI disclosure showed that the chain need not be novel. Ordinary credential theft was enough once the default identity was over-scoped.

Three implications follow for policy.

First, least privilege is the control that converts a dangerous tool into a bounded one. Saltzer and Schroeder stated the rule in 1975: every program and every user should operate with the least set of privileges necessary to complete the job. NIST SP 800-53 and zero-trust guidance restated it for federal systems. Agentic deployments violate it by habit. Case reviews of documented agent incidents find excessive privilege in roughly three-quarters of events, indirect prompt injection in a large majority, and a missing or bypassed human approval in essentially all of them. Prompt injection remains unsolved at the text layer. OWASP has ranked it the leading large-language-model application risk since 2023 precisely because the model does not separate trusted instructions from untrusted content. Filtering reduces noise. It does not bound damage. The reliable reduction in blast radius is architectural: a distinct, attestable identity for each agent; a named human owner; task-scoped rights; short-lived credentials; no outbound write tools for agents that read mail, the web, or retrieved documents; and a human gate on payments, production changes, permission changes, and release of sensitive data. Smaller firms can start with that list. Critical operators should be held to it through procurement and sector guidance, with AI confined to controlled interfaces, independent monitoring, and tested recovery. Standing authority over a safety system is not an efficiency feature. It is an unpriced liability.

Second, fear is reduced by a visible boundary, not by a new permit. Households connect assistants to email, cloud storage, and financial accounts because the product asks for the keys and the convenience is immediate. The public rule that matches the evidence is simple enough to repeat: review the permissions before connecting mail or banking, require a second check on any payment or credential change, and disconnect an agent that requests broader access. Firms need the institutional version of the same rule—an inventory, an owner, a log, and a kill switch. Executive Order 14409 already draws the public line in the right place. It directs an AI cybersecurity clearinghouse, in voluntary collaboration with developers and critical-infrastructure operators, to coordinate vulnerability discovery and remediation. It contemplates a classified benchmark for covered frontier models and a voluntary pre-release window for trusted partners. It tells the Justice Department to prioritize enforcement against people who use these systems to break into computers, steal data, or commit fraud. And it states that nothing in the order authorizes mandatory licensing, preclearance, or permitting for the development or release of models. That last sentence is the conservative constraint. Criminals do not file for permission. Defensive models are delayed by the same gate that is supposed to restrain offensive ones. A clearinghouse that drifts into a de facto approval desk would contradict the order’s text and recreate the bureaucracy the order refused.

Third, enforcement and measurement have to stay honest or the argument collapses. FBI reporting establishes generative systems as a fraud multiplier: synthetic text, voice clones, and video make impersonation cheaper. Those are reasons to prosecute wire fraud, unauthorized access, and impersonation, and to teach the public to slow down under pressure. They are not reasons to license weights. Methodological gaps belong in the same account. Survey respondents are security and IT staff, not a random sample of firms. Average incident narratives conceal how many organizations still lack a real-time agent registry. A paper that cites only the 53 percent and omits the detection failure, the shared-credential pattern, and the limits of the sample will be read as selective. Measurement honesty is an asset. It denies opponents the charge of concealment and keeps the remedy on the comparative record: identity controls and criminal law versus a preclearance regime that does not bind the offender.

Communications follow from the same evidence. Boards and the public conflate “AI is powerful” with “AI must be licensed.” The effective close is a small set of repeated comparisons—the agent as a badged contractor rather than a master key, the share of documented incidents that combine excess privilege with missing human approval, the June 2026 order’s explicit refusal of a license, and the dollar path of AI-enabled fraud already inside the FBI’s complaint system. Model benchmarks and narratives about an intelligence race are supporting context. They are not the lead. The lead is whether a manipulated email can move money.

Risks should be stated plainly. Synthetic impersonation will keep improving even if domestic agents are tightly scoped; global criminal tooling does not wait on U.S. procurement standards. State breach laws, sector regulators, and contracts will do more day-to-day work than a single statute, and a federal identity standard that ignores them will be ignored in turn. If the clearinghouse becomes an approval queue, industry participation will thin and the defensive purpose will fail. If firms inventory agents but leave standing privilege, they will meet the letter and miss the control. If agencies claim unilateral authority to preclear models, the end of Chevron deference cuts against them, and litigation will delay any security effect past the operational need. None of these risks argues for inaction. Each argues for sequencing: unique identity, task scope, short-lived credentials, human gates, and logs first; clearinghouse and voluntary frontier evaluation second; prosecution continuously. Statute should restate what the order already says, so a later administration cannot invent a license from a security memorandum.

Rivera’s diagnosis is correct on the failure mode and incomplete if it stops at exhortation. America is not facing a choice between the AI build-out and digital security. It is facing a choice between bounded authority and standing privilege. Agents that search, draft, and call tools are already inside enterprises. Scope violations are already common. Prompt injection has no reliable filter. Default cloud identities have already failed closed only because they were never closed. The historical literature from Bell-LaPadula and Saltzer and Schroeder through the Orange Book, FISMA, the Target and OPM breaches, NIST SP 800-207, and Executive Order 14028 supports a measured claim: systems fail at the speed of their privileges, and audit without revocation is a record of the loss rather than a prevention of it. The 2023–2026 agent literature supports a sharper claim: indirect injection plus a write tool plus broad standing access is the pattern that turns a document into an incident.

The synthesis is a program ambitious about defensive coordination, restrained about licensing, and explicit about the permissions households and operators can verify. Permanent identity discipline—not a one-time security pledge, and not a government dividend of new bureaucracy—is the sustainable control. Implement the June 2026 clearinghouse. Keep frontier evaluation voluntary and classified, with confidentiality and intellectual-property terms. Prosecute the fraud and the intrusion. Require the badge, the narrow task, the short-lived credential, and the human gate. That package answers the fear without smothering the technology that American firms are already using to find vulnerabilities faster than attackers publish them. The most important question is not how intelligent these systems become. It is whether the authority they hold can still be revoked by the people who granted it.

Statement on restrictions faced by cartoonists Satish Acharya and Manjul on Instagram

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly condemns the restrictions faced by cartoonists @satishacharya and @MANJULtoons on Instagram. On 26th September, Manjul’s cartoon on the Election Commission was restricted in India “pursuant to a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement.” 

Satish Acharya also repeatedly faced takedowns of his posts on Instagram, and on 28th September, his account got restricted in India. The notification shared by the cartoonist stated that the platform had to “repeatedly restrict access to content posted” by him “pursuant to legal requirements.”

In March 2026, Satish also received two notifications from @X stating that @GoI_MeitY had ordered the platform to block his content. He also received a notification from X about a content takedown request from the Cyber Crime Department of the Mumbai Police. These cartoons depicted India’s stance on US-Israel bombing on Iran and the killing of its supreme leader. Another cartoon showed the arms of state actors forming a human chain around billionaire Gautam Adani with the caption “Ek hain to safe hain.”

These notifications also stated that the platform could not provide him with additional information due to legal restrictions. This lack of transparency makes it particularly difficult to challenge a blocking order. While notifications issued by X identified the authorities that ordered the takedowns, Instagram did not disclose which authorities had ordered the takedowns. In such instances, before a creator can even consider approaching a court, they may first have to determine which government authority issued the order, under what legal provision it was issued, and what specific content or reasoning formed the basis for it. Without access to this information, exercising the right to challenge the restriction becomes significantly harder. 

Even when the information is available, going to court requires time, money, and legal assistance. All of these resources may not even be available for cartoonists, independent creators, or students. For someone facing multiple takedown orders, challenging each restriction individually can become an exhausting and expensive exercise.

@scroll_in’s article on the restrictions faced by Satish Acharya stated that the cartoonist attempted to challenge Meta’s action but was unable to reach Instagram’s help centre due to its automated grievance redressal systems and the lack of access to human support. Meta’s AI Support Assistant provides ‘In-App Appeal’ as the ‘primary method for challenging a content decision.’ However, this method is not a statutory remedy, amenable to further challenge at the Grievance Appellate Committee level. The prescribed procedure of approaching the Grievance Officer through Meta’s official reporting form does not provide a method to report the takedown of content, either for violations of Meta Community Standards, Terms of Service, or takedowns through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements.”

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also observed that the Grievance Officer email address available on the website can only be used to enquire about the grievance redressal mechanism and not to file a Grievance Officer report. This also creates a structural barrier to access further remedies, such as approaching the Grievance Appellate Committee, which mandatorily requires a Grievance Officer report to be filed prior to filing an appeal.

In the past few months, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has recorded similar instances of restrictions faced by other cartoonists in India. In August 2026, @cartoonistrrs's posts showing a comical representation of the PM’s viral reel received a takedown notice, and @cartoonistvish faced 4 takedown orders for his cartoon criticising Prime Minister Narender Modi’s foreign travels during domestic issues. Even a simple satire by @BagchiAsh, showing the PM with a Melody chocolate on his forehead, was restricted on Meta.

Over time, such instances of censorship can have consequences far beyond individual takedowns. When creators repeatedly see their work removed without clear explanations and realise that the only meaningful way to challenge the decision may be through costly legal proceedings, they may begin to censor themselves. The uncertainty surrounding what can be taken down and the difficulty of fighting back when takedowns happen can eventually discourage people from creating altogether. If the cost of speaking becomes too high and the consequences too unpredictable, creators may censor themselves or give up on their art entirely.

The increasing trend of censorship of cartoons and political humour is deeply concerning, particularly because it points to a shrinking space for dissent in India. The right to freedom of speech and expression is a fundamental right, and the ability to question, criticise and even ridicule those in power is an essential part of a democratic society. Dissent may be uncomfortable for governments, but discomfort cannot be the basis for silencing it.

The Government should also ensure that the users are provided with meaningful, accessible, and timely avenues for content takedowns and account restrictions.

text:
The debate surrounding #Starlink in #India is not really about internet speeds, rural connectivity or even Elon Musk.

It is about #sovereignty 
History teaches us that nations rarely lose strategic autonomy overnight. More often, dependence develops gradually through systems, networks and institutions that become too important to function without.

The #BritishEastIndiaCompany did not arrive in India as a conquering army. It arrived as a commercial enterprise promising trade, access to global markets and economic opportunity. Over time, commercial influence evolved into political leverage, strategic control and eventually colonial rule.

The world of the 21st century is different, but the underlying principle remains relevant.

Today, influence is exercised not only through territory and military power but through data, communications infrastructure, digital platforms, satellite networks and technological dependence.

This is where Starlink becomes a strategic question rather than merely a telecommunications project.

Supporters correctly point out that satellite internet can transform connectivity in remote regions, improve disaster response and bridge digital divides. These are real benefits.

However, strategic planners must also ask a different set of questions:
“Who controls the network?
Who ultimately decides where service is available?”

What happens during a geopolitical crisis?
Can a sovereign nation guarantee uninterrupted access if the infrastructure is owned, operated and controlled by a foreign private entity?

The Ukraine conflict offers a powerful example.
Reports revealed that Starlink services were restricted during a planned Ukrainian operation targeting Russian naval assets near Crimea. The result was that the operation could not proceed as intended because the communications network required for execution was unavailable.

Regardless of one’s views on the decision, the larger geopolitical lesson is clear:
A private company and its leadership possessed the ability to influence the operational options available to a sovereign state during an active conflict.

That reality should concern every serious strategic planner in the world.
The issue is not whether Elon Musk was right or wrong.

The issue is whether any nation should place critical national communications infrastructure in a position where ultimate operational control rests outside its sovereign authority.

For India, this question carries even greater significance.

India faces an increasingly contested security environment stretching from the Himalayas to the Indian Ocean. #Communications resilience is not merely an economic requirement; it is a #nationalsecurity necessity.

This does not mean rejecting foreign technology.
India has benefited enormously from international investment, technology partnerships and global integration.

But integration should never become dependence.
The ideal outcome is not isolation but strategic balance: encouraging innovation while ensuring robust regulatory oversight, #dataprotection, local compliance requirements and #sovereigncontrol mechanisms.

The lesson of the #EastIndiaCompany is often misunderstood.
The danger was never trade itself.

The danger was allowing critical leverage to accumulate outside Indian control.

As technology becomes the new arena of geopolitical competition, nations must remember a simple principle:
Infrastructure creates dependence.
Dependence creates leverage.
Leverage creates influence.

And influence, if left unchecked, can eventually challenge sovereignty itself.

India was colonised once through commerce and influence.
The next challenge, if it ever comes, will not arrive on sailing ships.

It will arrive through networks, platforms, satellites and systems that become too important to question

That is why the Starlink debate is not merely abt connectivity.
It is about ensuring that 🇮🇳’s digital future remains firmly under Indian sovereign control #JaiHind

Expected deeper research from @ARKInvest  on this one. @wintonARK 's Starlink thesis has holes that spectrum law and physics won't let you ignore. If a fund this caliber is missing the fundamentals of D2D, it shows how poorly understood this space still is.
Let me address it directly.
His core claim: $SPCX  becomes the first truly global telecom, launches its own cellular brand, satellite-default with cellular failover.

Four problems.
1) Spectrum is sovereign. To run a global cellular brand, SpaceX needs direct-to-consumer spectrum in every country. Each nation licenses its own. You can't "amortize connectivity across the world" when you need 195 separate national grants and most governments won't hand a foreign company their citizens' airwaves. India just blocked Starlink for this exact reason. Europe reserved spectrum for local operators. Japan is building its own.
2) The capacity math is backwards. "Satellite default, cellular failover" violates physics. One satellite beam covers hundreds of square miles, sharing capacity across everyone in it. A cell tower covers a few hundred meters with orders of magnitude more capacity. Satellite can't be the DEFAULT in any populated area - there isn't enough capacity density. @SpaceX 's own VP said it: Starlink Mobile is "not meant to replace terrestrial infrastructure."
3) Sovereignty is moving the opposite direction. Your thesis needs governments to allow one foreign company to own national connectivity. That's exactly what's being blocked worldwide right now. The trend isn't toward a global SpaceX telecom - it's away from it.
4) Carriers won't be the failover. "Failover to cellular" needs roaming deals with the carriers SpaceX is trying to replace. Why would @ATT &T let SpaceX use its network as a backup for a product built to disintermediate AT&T? They wouldn't. That's why all 3 US carriers formed a JV around $ASTS instead - a partner that extends them, not one that replaces them.

The global telecom future is real. But it's not one company owning the world's connectivity. It's local carriers, sovereign spectrum, and a satellite layer that works THROUGH them. That's the model $ASTS  was built for. And it's the model governments are actively choosing.

Happy to debate any of this if you've got a counter. I'll bring the FCC filings.

grok: what countries have banned starlink and what are their international freedom scores

No country with a high Freedom House score has imposed a hard ban on Starlink. The places where it is explicitly blocked or blacklisted are almost all rated Not Free, with very low scores on political rights and civil liberties.

Freedom House’s Freedom in the World 2026 (covering 2025) uses a 0–100 scale. Higher is freer. Status is Free / Partly Free / Not Free.⁠Freedomhouse
Explicitly banned or blacklisted

These appear in Starlink’s own availability data and reporting as hard blocks (geofenced, no license, import bans, or official prohibition of terminals):
Country / territoryFreedom House 2026StatusNotes on Starlink
North Korea3Not FreeTotal isolation; no commercial satellite internet of this type.
Belarus7Not FreeNever licensed; regime has said use is not permitted.
Afghanistan8Not FreeBlacklisted; Taliban-era restrictions.
China9Not FreeUnlicensed foreign satellite comms banned; enforcement includes ships in territorial waters. Ban extends to Hong Kong and Macao under PRC telecom rules.
Cuba9Not FreeOften listed as unavailable / restricted.
Iran10Not FreeTerminals formally prohibited; no authorization to operate.
Russia12Not FreeOfficial ban; 2026 decree banned import of foreign satellite terminals on national-security grounds and named Starlink.
Syria~10 (was ~5, +5 in 2025)Not FreeBlacklisted; also tied to sanctions / parent-regime issues.
Hong Kong scores 41 (Partly Free) but is covered by China’s ban.⁠Mappr

These governments treat an independent, foreign-controlled constellation as a threat to information control, data sovereignty, or national security. That tracks with how they treat the open internet generally.
Not the same as a “ban”
Several other countries have denied licenses or sit in regulatory limbo for ownership rules, local-partner requirements, or security reviews—not a blanket geopolitical ban:
Namibia — license refused (51% local ownership rule). Not in the hard-blacklist group.
South Africa — stalled on Black Economic Empowerment ownership rules.
India — license progress but final security clearance delayed at times.
Others in limbo or “coming soon”: parts of North Africa, some Gulf states, etc.

DRC banned then reversed. Papua New Guinea had a legal fight that later eased. Those are regulatory fights, not the same category as Russia or China.

Pattern: Hard bans cluster at the bottom of the Freedom House scale (single digits to low teens). Countries that score in the 80s–100s (Canada, much of Europe, Japan, etc.) have licensed Starlink or are in the process of doing so. The correlation is not accidental: the service is useful precisely where terrestrial networks are weak and where governments want to keep a closed information environment.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

I discovered a sudden issue in the 0.6x ultra-wide camera of my Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra. The phone was never dropped, never mishandled. After researching online, I found MANY users reporting the exact same issue with the new 50MP ultra-wide sensor. Reddit, YouTube, Samsung Community — same problem everywhere.

Because my device was out of warranty, the Dharampeth service centre immediately gave me a ₹4000 quotation instead of acknowledging a possible manufacturing defect.

After endless emails, Samsung support kept repeating: “You have to pay.”

Why should customers pay for Samsung’s hardware failure?

After getting exhausted, I posted on X on 26 April tagging Samsung Electronics India. Only then did they react. Customer Experience Manager Kajal contacted me, and after I shared proof from multiple users online, Samsung finally offered a 73% discount.

I accepted because I was mentally tired of fighting.

On 6 May, I submitted the device. On 7 May, I collected it after paying ₹1000.

Camera fixed?
YES.

New disaster?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF THE VERY NEXT MORNING.

I informed the service centre on WhatsApp. They ignored the messages.

Visited again on 11 May — they “fixed” it.

Two days later?
BACK PANEL AGAIN COMING OFF.

Visited again on 14 May — this time the behavior became shocking.

Instead of accepting poor repair quality, staff started accusing ME of removing the back panel with sharp objects. They checked the device and found ZERO evidence.

Then they saw BGMI installed.

And suddenly their excuse became:
“BGMI is a third-party app. Using third-party apps voids warranty and service.”

Imagine buying one of Samsung’s most powerful flagship phones and being told GAMING can void service support.

When I asked for a written denial letter, they REFUSED.

When I started recording for proof, they stopped answering questions and began ignoring me completely.

I had no option left except calling the police.

ONLY after police intervention did the entire attitude of the service centre change. Suddenly:
“We never denied service.”
“We are ready to repair.”

They even requested police officers to convince me to delete the videos I recorded.

After another repair attempt, they told me:
“Do not use BGMI for 12 hours.”

I followed everything they said.

Result?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF AGAIN.

Since then I have been continuously emailing Samsung support and Kajal from customer experience, asking for a permanent solution or replacement because I cannot travel 13KM repeatedly for the SAME ISSUE.

Today again, after being told to visit the service centre, they AGAIN accused me and AGAIN refused service while refusing to provide any written denial.

The moment I started recording, everyone went silent.

This is the reality of Samsung’s “premium flagship experience” in Nagpur.

Customers are blamed.
Manufacturing defects are ignored.
Poor repairs are repeated.
Written denials are refused.
And consumers are forced into endless visits until they give up.

Absolutely shameful. @SamsungMobile @SamsungIndia

By Skye Jacobs  Today 2:36 PM    
Your ChatGPT conversations could end up in court, and they're not protected
Chatbot conversations lack the legal privilege covering communications with lawyers, doctors, and therapists

 Add TechSpot 
   📷
Serving tech enthusiasts for over 25 years.  
 TechSpot means tech analysis and advice you can trust.
The takeaway: Private  conversations with AI chatbots are increasingly being used in court  cases, creating a new source of evidence for police, prosecutors, and  civil litigants. These records can expose a user's intentions, private  thoughts, and sensitive disclosures, yet they generally receive none of  the legal confidentiality protections afforded to conversations with  lawyers, doctors, or therapists.
ChatGPT and similar tools are often used for personal questions, legal worries, health concerns, and emotional support. Those conversations can feel private, but they may be accessible through a phone search, a  subpoena, discovery in a lawsuit, or a report by the AI company itself.

A review by The Washington Post found chatbot conversations cited in  12 public court cases over the past two years. The number is likely  higher because much of the evidence collected during investigations and  lawsuits never becomes public.

One case involved a teenager identified in court records as R.K.C.,  who sued Meta, Snap, TikTok, and YouTube in 2023. He alleged that their  platforms contributed to social media addiction and mental health  problems.

Defense lawyers obtained his ChatGPT history during the case. In one  October 2024 conversation, R.K.C. asked the chatbot to explain a  statement from his father about a possible settlement.

"My dad Said that I'm will get a settlement worth of  1million dollar," he wrote. "He said that If that doesn't make me happy  what does. What does he mean."

// Related Stories

 Ring rolls out new encryption system that could limit what it can hand over to police 
 AI is driving an "expertise recession" as people increasingly question professional advice 

R.K.C.'s lawyers settled with Snap, TikTok, and YouTube by late July.  They also dropped the case against Meta, saying they were concerned  about putting the teenager through a long trial. The companies denied  his claims. Mike Morgan, a partner at Morgan & Morgan, said the  ChatGPT messages did not affect the outcome of the case.
📷

Credit: The Washington Post

Morgan said young people may share more with a  chatbot than they would with family members, friends, or therapists. "A  fifteen-year-old may type things into a chatbot that he may not say to a  therapist, a parent, or a friend, and he does it without realizing that  it could end up in a defense expert's report," he said in a statement.

Chatbot records have also become part of criminal cases.

In Palm Beach County, Florida, OpenAI contacted the  FBI after a ChatGPT user repeatedly described plans to harm an  ex-girlfriend, according to a police affidavit. The FBI passed the  information to local police, who identified the woman and found that the  user, Darren Zhou, had sent her anonymous messages after their  relationship ended.

Police said the ChatGPT conversations supported the  credibility of the threats. Zhou was arrested in May and charged with  stalking and making electronic threats. He pleaded guilty this month and  was sentenced to eight years of probation.

OpenAI has said it uses software to detect  conversations that may involve dangerous behavior. Those conversations  can be reviewed by staff. If reviewers determine there is "an imminent  and credible risk of harm to others," the company may contact law  enforcement.

The company has not said how often it makes such  reports. Its transparency data, however, shows a sharp increase in  government and law-enforcement requests for user information. OpenAI  disclosed data from more than 80 accounts during the second half of  2025, more than four times the total from the same period a year  earlier.

In many cases, police do not need to obtain records from an AI company. They find the conversations on a person's phone.

Michael Price, litigation director of the Fourth  Amendment Center at the National Association of Criminal Defense  Lawyers, said people often agree to let officers search their phones. In  most situations, people have the right to refuse a search unless police  have a warrant.

"The short answer is that most people consent," Price told The Washington Post. "They shouldn't, but they do."

📷

That happened in the case of Ryan Schaefer, a  Missouri State University student accused of damaging 17 cars in a  campus parking lot. According to police records, Schaefer agreed to let  officers search his phone. They found ChatGPT messages he sent shortly  after the alleged vandalism.

"How f----d am i bro," Schaefer wrote. "What if i smahsed the s--- oitta mutlipls cars."

He later wrote: "Is there any way they could know it was me."

Schaefer later pleaded guilty to felony property damage and was sentenced in July to five years of probation.

AI chats can also be pulled into civil lawsuits  through the discovery process. In a Michigan employment case, a tire  salesman's former employer alleged that he had taken customers after  joining a rival company. The salesman had asked ChatGPT whether deleted  Yahoo emails could still be retrieved, including through a court  subpoena.

The employer argued that the messages showed he had  tried to hide evidence. A judge later ordered him to pay an undetermined  amount in attorneys' fees and allowed the lawsuit to continue.

Chatbot exchanges do not have the legal protections  that apply to conversations with lawyers, doctors, or therapists. OpenAI  CEO Sam Altman has said AI conversations should have stronger privacy  protections because people increasingly use chatbots for sensitive  matters. Courts have not recognized that type of privilege.

A federal judge in New York made that clear in a case  involving financial executive Bradley Heppner. Heppner argued that  prosecutors should not be allowed to review his conversations with  Anthropic's Claude about potential fraud defenses. The judge ruled that  the chats were not protected because Claude is not a lawyer and  Heppner's attorneys had not told him to consult the chatbot.

Heppner was convicted in May of securities fraud, wire fraud, and other charges.

The issue may grow as AI tools take on more tasks for  users and gain access to more personal data. Andrew Ferguson, a law  professor at George Washington University who studies digital  surveillance, said chatbot records may be only the beginning.

"Your entire world is going to now be available for police," Ferguson said.

text:
India's platforms are legally required to notify users when their content gets taken down by government order — but compliance is spotty at best.
The rule exists under the Information Technology Act's intermediary framework. When a platform receives a government takedown notice, users are supposed to get an explanation: what was removed, why, and which authority issued it.
In practice, most platforms either ignore this entirely or send vague notices after the fact. No timeline is enforced. No standardized format exists. Users often discover their content is gone only when they try to access it.
Former MeitY (Ministry of Electronics and IT) cyber-law officials have flagged this gap repeatedly. The logic was simple: transparency about state censorship creates a paper trail, deters overreach, and lets users contest removals.
But India's digital ecosystem treats the notification rule as optional. WhatsApp doesn't notify for group bans. Twitter (now X) batches notices weeks later. YouTube compliance varies by region. TikTok, before its ban, rarely proactively informed users.
The enforcement gap matters because:
• There is no penalty structure — platforms face no fines or license consequences for skipping notification.
• Users have no realistic way to challenge removals without knowing they happened or why.
• Government agencies know the lack of oversight means takedowns go undocumented.
• A parallel system of private censorship operates without the judicial review that formal bans would trigger.
The fix would require either stricter intermediary rules with real penalties, or a centralized notification registry — both politically difficult in India's current regulatory environment.
As government content moderation requests accelerate globally, India's notification gap is becoming a template for how to make state censorship functionally invisible.

#MeitY #India #PlatformRegulation

text:
Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

Heartiest congratulations to the athletes from Karnataka who have brought pride to the State while adding to the nation’s glory by winning medals at the 20th Asian Games being held in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.

It gives me immense happiness to see Karnataka’s young talent Ayush Shetty, a member of the Indian men’s badminton team, win a bronze medal. Ayush has already proven his talent on the international stage at a young age, and I wish him even greater success and many more achievements in the years ahead.

The achievement of M.R. Poovamma, the proud Kannadiga who was part of the Indian team that won silver in the 4×400 metres mixed relay, is equally special. Her experience, discipline and long-standing commitment to Indian athletics continue to inspire young sportspersons.

The Indian women’s cricket team winning India’s first gold medal at the Asian Games is a moment of celebration for the entire country. Special congratulations to Karnataka’s Shreyanka Patil, who was part of this historic success. This victory is yet another testament to the confidence and ability of our women athletes.

The achievement of Tilottama Sen, a member of the Indian team that won silver in the women’s 50-metre rifle shooting event, is another proud moment for Karnataka. Winning an international medal in a sport that demands immense concentration and dedication is truly commendable.

The achievements of Ayush Shetty, M.R. Poovamma, Shreyanka Patil and Tilottama Sen will inspire thousands of young athletes across Karnataka. They have once again shown that, with the right opportunities and encouragement, our children can excel on the world stage.

Behind every medal lie years of hard work, sacrifice, discipline and continuous practice. The support of families, guidance from coaches and encouragement received at different stages are also an integral part of every sporting achievement. Recognising that effort with the honour and support it deserves is both the duty and responsibility of the Government.

Karnataka has no shortage of sporting talent. It has repeatedly been proven that, with the right opportunities, quality coaching, good infrastructure and necessary financial support, our children can excel on any international platform.

Rather than recognising athletes only after they win medals, our Government is giving greater priority to identifying talent at an early stage and providing appropriate training and encouragement. Our objective is to ensure continuous access to good coaches, scientific training and the sporting facilities athletes need.

Sporting opportunities should not be confined to urban areas. Talented children from rural regions and ordinary families must also receive equal opportunities. The Sports Department is therefore working to identify talent from every corner of the State and provide them with proper training and platforms to compete.

The support system for athletes performing at the national and international levels is being further strengthened through incentives, financial assistance, training and employment opportunities. Young people choosing sport as a career must have confidence and financial security. We are working to create an environment in which they can continue their sporting journey without uncertainty.

Karnataka athletes participating in the Olympics, Commonwealth Games, Asian Games and Asian Para Games are being provided a special incentive of ₹5 lakh each. Medal winners are further honoured with an additional cash award of ₹15 lakh.

Young people who excel in sports must have the confidence and security to choose sport itself as a career. Already, 13 athletes who have won medals in international competitions have been appointed to Group ‘A’ and Group ‘B’ government posts through special recruitment. In addition, the reservation for sportspersons in the State Police Department has been increased from 2% to 3%.

To ensure that students interested in sports are not forced to choose between education and sport, those participating in State and national-level competitions have been granted 15% attendance exemption, while those participating in international-level competitions receive 25% attendance exemption. This enables them to pursue their education smoothly alongside their sporting ambitions.

Strong infrastructure is equally important for sporting excellence. In this direction, 32 stadiums across the State are being developed at a cost of ₹36 crore. A decision has also been taken to systematically organise Dasara sports competitions from the taluk level, covering kabaddi, athletics and rural sports, thereby creating greater opportunities for rural talent.

Through these measures, greater emphasis is being placed on strengthening Karnataka’s sporting infrastructure, identifying and nurturing talent, and preparing young athletes for national and international competitions. Our goal is to make Karnataka one of the country’s leading States in sports as well.

Once again, heartiest congratulations to Ayush Shetty, M.R. Poovamma, Shreyanka Patil and Tilottama Sen, the medal winners at the Asian Games 2026. Your achievements have made Kannadigas proud. I wish you even greater success in your sporting journeys ahead. The State Government will always stand behind you and provide the necessary support and encouragement.

With the Asian Games set to continue for a few more days, I wish many more athletes from India and Karnataka participating across various disciplines the very best. May they win more medals and further enhance the pride of both the country and the State.

text:
The Delhi Police's takedown drive against posts critical of the Prime Minister is unconstitutional. 

New Delhi, 27 July 2026

Media reports today state that the Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove posts, videos, memes and reels containing remarks it describes as "abusive", "offensive" and "objectionable" towards the Prime Minister, uploaded during the student protests at Jantar Mantar and after the 'Sansad Chalo' march of 20 July 2026. At least three platforms have reportedly received notices. Several posts have already been taken down. A dedicated police team is monitoring social media to identify further content, and reports indicate that criminal proceedings are contemplated against those who posted it. No order has been published. While reports indicate the notices invoke the Information Technology Act, the specific provision relied upon and the text of the notices remain undisclosed. 

The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns this takedown drive and calls for the notices to be disclosed and withdrawn.

On the reports available, the content being removed is political expression. The movement at Jantar Mantar has been conducted as much through reels, memes, posters and digital artwork as through assembly on the ground. This is how a digital native generation raised online speaks about accountability. As per Article 19(2) restrictions on speech only on eight specified grounds. Offensiveness is not one of them. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act precisely because expressions such as "grossly offensive" and causing "annoyance" were vague, subjective, and swept protected speech within their net. Eleven years later, the Delhi Police is applying the same standard through informal notices and legal powers which are not being publicly disclosed. 

As per existing practices there are two routes for removing online content. The first is Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules, 2009, which requires a reasoned order, committee review, and notice to the originator, as the Delhi High Court affirmed in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). The second is Section 79(3)(b), which Shreya Singhal read down to require a court order or a government notification strictly confined to Article 19(2) grounds. If these notices were routed through the Sahyog Portal, they rest on a regime whose constitutionality remains under challenge before multiple High Courts. However, even if it is used police notices citing offensiveness satisfy neither. 

Reports that platforms were told the content violates "their policies" make the defect worse, the police have no mandate to enforce the community guidelines of private companies. Unpublished directions are also contrary to Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637, which requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published so that they can be challenged. If the underlying theory is defamation of the Prime Minister, the police have no role at all. Defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognizable offence, prosecuted only on a complaint by the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. 

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must publish every notice issued, the legal provision invoked, and the list of URLs affected.

2. Notices directed at satire, criticism, and political commentary must be withdrawn. Any removal must follow the procedures under Section 69A or a judicial order.

3. No criminal proceedings should be initiated against persons for speech that does not meet the constitutional threshold of incitement.

4. Platforms must decline requests unsupported by valid legal orders, notify affected users, and disclose the number of government demands in their transparency reports.

Students who question an examination system are exercising their fundamental rights and deleting their posts will not delete their questions.

Reports referred to:

1. Times of India, "Delhi Police orders removal of offensive posts against PM Narendra Modi linked to NEET paper leak protests", 27 July 2026
2. News18, "Delhi Police Issues Notices To Social Media Platforms Over Offensive Posts Against PM Modi During Jantar Mantar Protest", 27 July 2026

Statement on restrictions faced by cartoonists Satish Acharya and Manjul on Instagram

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly condemns the restrictions faced by cartoonists @satishacharya and @MANJULtoons on Instagram. On 26th September, Manjul’s cartoon on the Election Commission was restricted in India “pursuant to a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement.” 

Satish Acharya also repeatedly faced takedowns of his posts on Instagram, and on 28th September, his account got restricted in India. The notification shared by the cartoonist stated that the platform had to “repeatedly restrict access to content posted” by him “pursuant to legal requirements.”

In March 2026, Satish also received two notifications from @X stating that @GoI_MeitY had ordered the platform to block his content. He also received a notification from X about a content takedown request from the Cyber Crime Department of the Mumbai Police. These cartoons depicted India’s stance on US-Israel bombing on Iran and the killing of its supreme leader. Another cartoon showed the arms of state actors forming a human chain around billionaire Gautam Adani with the caption “Ek hain to safe hain.”

These notifications also stated that the platform could not provide him with additional information due to legal restrictions. This lack of transparency makes it particularly difficult to challenge a blocking order. While notifications issued by X identified the authorities that ordered the takedowns, Instagram did not disclose which authorities had ordered the takedowns. In such instances, before a creator can even consider approaching a court, they may first have to determine which government authority issued the order, under what legal provision it was issued, and what specific content or reasoning formed the basis for it. Without access to this information, exercising the right to challenge the restriction becomes significantly harder. 

Even when the information is available, going to court requires time, money, and legal assistance. All of these resources may not even be available for cartoonists, independent creators, or students. For someone facing multiple takedown orders, challenging each restriction individually can become an exhausting and expensive exercise.

@scroll_in’s article on the restrictions faced by Satish Acharya stated that the cartoonist attempted to challenge Meta’s action but was unable to reach Instagram’s help centre due to its automated grievance redressal systems and the lack of access to human support. Meta’s AI Support Assistant provides ‘In-App Appeal’ as the ‘primary method for challenging a content decision.’ However, this method is not a statutory remedy, amenable to further challenge at the Grievance Appellate Committee level. The prescribed procedure of approaching the Grievance Officer through Meta’s official reporting form does not provide a method to report the takedown of content, either for violations of Meta Community Standards, Terms of Service, or takedowns through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements.”

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also observed that the Grievance Officer email address available on the website can only be used to enquire about the grievance redressal mechanism and not to file a Grievance Officer report. This also creates a structural barrier to access further remedies, such as approaching the Grievance Appellate Committee, which mandatorily requires a Grievance Officer report to be filed prior to filing an appeal.

In the past few months, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has recorded similar instances of restrictions faced by other cartoonists in India. In August 2026, @cartoonistrrs's posts showing a comical representation of the PM’s viral reel received a takedown notice, and @cartoonistvish faced 4 takedown orders for his cartoon criticising Prime Minister Narender Modi’s foreign travels during domestic issues. Even a simple satire by @BagchiAsh, showing the PM with a Melody chocolate on his forehead, was restricted on Meta.

Over time, such instances of censorship can have consequences far beyond individual takedowns. When creators repeatedly see their work removed without clear explanations and realise that the only meaningful way to challenge the decision may be through costly legal proceedings, they may begin to censor themselves. The uncertainty surrounding what can be taken down and the difficulty of fighting back when takedowns happen can eventually discourage people from creating altogether. If the cost of speaking becomes too high and the consequences too unpredictable, creators may censor themselves or give up on their art entirely.

The increasing trend of censorship of cartoons and political humour is deeply concerning, particularly because it points to a shrinking space for dissent in India. The right to freedom of speech and expression is a fundamental right, and the ability to question, criticise and even ridicule those in power is an essential part of a democratic society. Dissent may be uncomfortable for governments, but discomfort cannot be the basis for silencing it.

The Government should also ensure that the users are provided with meaningful, accessible, and timely avenues for content takedowns and account restrictions.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.
